claims.text: A data-driven or machine-learning model with expandable features can accurately identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach is intended for high-entropy alloys in an as-cast or annealed state.
The model is trained using high-entropy-alloy compositions, microstructures, and corresponding thermal-conductivity measurements.
The training dataset contains at least 100 samples.
Feature engineering is used to expand the model's feature space.
Thermal conductivity depends on complex relationships among alloy composition and microstructure.
The machine-learning model captures relationships among alloy composition, microstructure, and thermal conductivity.
Learning patterns correlated with low phonon thermal conductivity enables accurate conductivity predictions.
The model will achieve a thermal-conductivity mean absolute error of 0.05 W/m-K or less.
An MAE of 0.05 W/m-K represents a 20% improvement over current predictions.
Traditional prediction methods currently have an MAE of 0.06 W/m-K.
The model is applicable only to high-entropy alloys containing between three and five principal elements.
The choice of machine-learning algorithm and feature-engineering technique may affect model performance.
The benchmark compares model predictions with experimentally measured thermal conductivity.
Thermal conductivity is measured using the laser-flash method, and microstructure is characterized using transmission electron microscopy.
The hypothesis is falsified if the model's MAE exceeds 0.07 W/m-K or if its predictions are not significantly better than current predictions.

contradictions.description: Reducing MAE from 0.06 to 0.05 W/m-K is a 16.7% reduction, not the claimed 20% improvement.

The predicted target is MAE at or below 0.05 W/m-K, but the numerical falsification threshold is only MAE above 0.07 W/m-K. Results between 0.05 and 0.07 can violate the quantitative prediction without necessarily meeting the stated numerical falsification rule.
